claims.text: The patient presents at 60 hours of age with a temperature of 38.1°C and poor feeding, which are clinical indicators consistent with suspected sepsis in the early-onset window. While the patient is in a hospital setting, the maternal GBS status is unknown, and red flags are not fully documented, necessitating a cautious clinical approach.

WHO 2024 does not endorse a single universal laboratory or clinical prediction algorithm for diagnosing neonatal sepsis. Instead, it notes that laboratory tests such as full blood count and CRP have historically been excluded from district-level algorithms due to availability issues, though point-of-care tests are becoming more common.

Systematic reviews cited in the guideline indicate that CRP and procalcitonin (PCT) demonstrate good discriminatory ability for diagnosing sepsis when blood culture is the reference standard, whereas erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) have poor discriminatory ability.

Diagnostic accuracy for CRP varies; one review reported that at a median specificity of 0.74, the sensitivity for CRP in neonates was 0.62. This suggests that while CRP is a useful biomarker, it is not a standalone definitive diagnostic tool and should be interpreted in the context of clinical presentation.

Regarding the duration of therapy, evidence suggests that CRP-based algorithms can shorten antibiotic treatment duration by approximately 1.15 to 1.45 days without significant differences in mortality or infection relapse. However, specific thresholds for stopping antibiotics should be guided by local protocols and clinical judgment rather than a single universal value.

Ongoing work is being conducted to integrate laboratory tests with clinical algorithms and to develop predictive tools to assist clinicians in determining when to stop antibiotics and rationalize therapy. Clinicians should monitor the patient's response to treatment and consider serial biomarker assessments if available, keeping in mind that no single algorithm is universally endorsed for diagnosis.

packet.guideline: WHO serious bacterial infections 2024 (EOS subset), EVALUATION ONLY
packet.evaluation_question: Does WHO 2024 endorse a hospital laboratory or clinical prediction algorithm to diagnose neonatal sepsis? Explain initial assessment without inventing a CBC or CRP threshold. Gestation 40 weeks; age 60 hours; setting hospital.

evidence.text: Two additional systematic reviews examined the diagnostic accuracy of laboratory biomarkers to diagnose culture-confirmed sepsis (88) or clinical or culture-confirmed sepsis (89) in infants aged 0–59 days at the time of presentation to health facilities. Brown et al. (2019) identified 20 studies of 1615 infants reporting upon diagnostic accuracy of CRP in neonates and reported that at median specificity (0.74), sensitivity was 0.62 (95% CI: 0.50 to 0.73) (88). Rees et al. (2023) examined CRP, procalcitonin (PCT), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and white cell count (WCC) in 134 studies, and concluded that CRP and PCT demonstrated good discriminatory ability to diagnose sepsis with blood culture as the reference

include laboratory tests due to the lack of availability of simple tests in district hospitals, such as full blood count and C-reactive protein (CRP). However, these tests have become more widely available and POC rapid “bedside” laboratory tests are becoming much more common (10, 75). There has also been much interest in how to integrate laboratory tests with IMCI and other clinical algorithms, and ongoing work to develop more sophisticated predictive algorithms and machine-learning tools to improve sepsis diagnosis, assist clinicians in determining when to stop antibiotics and rationalizing antibiotic therapy (75).

One further systematic review of seven studies and a total of 505 infants examined the use of CRP in decision-making for stopping antibiotic treatment in newborns diagnosed with sepsis (90). Petel et al. (2018) reported that CRP-based algorithms shortened antibiotic treatment duration by 1.45 days (95% CI: −2.61 to –0.28) in two RCTs, and by 1.15 days (95% CI: −2.06 to –0.24) in two cohort studies, with no differences in mortality or infection relapse in neonates (90).
(CRP of ≥ 60 mg/L, AUC: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.76 to 0.91, n=1339 neonates; and PCT of ≥ 0.5 ng/ml, AUC: 0.87, 95% CI: 0.70 to 0.92, n=617 neonates), while ESR and WCC had poor discriminatory ability (89).
